messages.content: Okay. So I Better idea for you. Can I log in to hulu and embed it On my website so I could stream it there?

No, you can't do that. Hulu's Terms of Service explicitly prohibit embedding their content on external sites, and they use DRM (Digital Rights Management) and authentication systems that prevent it.Here's the practical reality:Why it won't work:DRM protection: Hulu uses Widevine/PlayReady DRM. Their video streams are encrypted and require authenticated, whitelisted player environments.CORS & domain restrictions: Their APIs and video endpoints are locked to hulu.com domains. Requests from your domain will be blocked.Login/session binding: Even if you somehow got a player embed, the session is tied to Hulu's domain cookies and their own app environment. It would break immediately.What happens if you try:The embed would fail to load, orYou'd get a black screen / error, orHulu would detect it and potentially flag the accountWhat you can do instead:Hulu Watch Party — native feature for sharing viewing with friends/familyScreen share — Discord, Zoom, or browser tab sharing (for personal use, not public embedding)Build your own media server — if you have personal video files, use something like Plex, Jellyfin, or a custom HTML5 video player for your own contentIf you're building a private site for family video sharing (like you mentioned with your son and wife), the right path is uploading your own videos to a private host (or even a local NAS) and embedding those with a standard <video> tag or a lightweight player like Video.js.What's the actual goal — sharing personal family videos, or something else?                                               I fill my yeah. So I I built my own family site. It's hosted on either Vercel or fly fly dev. I have a bunch of videos on there. It seems Encrypted. I usually post them there on a video. Or Can post the link from my Proton drive, and they could stream it. Right? They're away on vacation.

Got it — so this is about your own family videos, not Hulu. Much simpler problem.Proton Drive links for streaming — yes, that works, with caveats:Proton Drive generates shareable links that recipients can stream directly from. Your family clicks the link, and Proton serves the video. No embedding needed on your site.However, if you want the videos to actually play inside your family site (not just link out to Proton), you have two paths:Path 1: Direct Proton Drive links on your siteKeep videos in Proton DriveGenerate share linksList them on your Vercel/Fly site as clickable linksFamily clicks → streams on Proton's playerPros: Zero bandwidth cost to you, Proton handles storage + streamingCons: Leaves your site, Proton's UI, not "embedded" in your pagePath 2: Actually embed the videos on your siteYou need a direct video URL (.mp4, .webm, etc.) that the browser can fetchProton Drive share links won't work for <video src="..."> embedding — they're HTML pages, not raw video filesOptions:Move videos to a storage service with direct links: Cloudflare R2, Backblaze B2, AWS S3 (cheapest for this use case)Or self-host: If you have a NAS or home server, reverse-proxy through something like NginxOr use a video-specific host: Mux, Cloudflare Stream (overkill for family stuff)The "encrypted" thing you mentioned:
If your current videos on the site "seem encrypted" and won't play, that's likely a codec or container issue — not actual encryption. Browsers only play specific formats:Safe: H.264 video + AAC audio in MP4 container (works everywhere)Problematic: HEVC/H.265, MKV, AV1 without proper encoding, or DRM-wrapped filesQuick question to get you the right fix:
Are your family videos currently on Proton Drive only, or are some already uploaded to your Vercel/Fly site and just not playing? And what format are they in (.mp4, .mov, .mkv)?                                               They wanna watch it on an LG smart TV. Does that have a browser? Or what app can they put watch it on?

Yes, LG smart TVs have a browser — it's usually called "Web Browser" in the app menu. It's a basic Chromium-based browser, so your Vercel/Fly site will load.But — it's a pretty bad experience for video:No full-screen support for <video> elements sometimesLimited codec support (H.264 MP4 is safest)Clunky navigation with the remoteMay struggle with large files or long videosBetter options for your family on an LG TV:1. Screen mirroring / casting (easiest)From phone: Use SmartShare (LG's built-in) or just screen mirror from iPhone/AndroidFrom laptop: Mirror the browser tab to the TVNo app needed, just works2. Send the Proton Drive link to their phone, cast to TVOpen Proton Drive link on phoneUse Chromecast or AirPlay to push to the LG TVMost LG TVs (2019+) have AirPlay built-in3. Add your site as a "web app" on the LG TVOpen the browser → go to your Vercel/Fly siteBookmark it or add to home screen if the TV supports itStill clunky, but one-click access4. External device (best experience)Fire Stick, Chromecast, Apple TV — plug into the LG TV, open browser or castWay better than the LG native browser for videoMy recommendation:
If they're on vacation and just need to watch family videos, send them the Proton Drive link + tell them to screen mirror from their phone to the TV. Zero setup, works on any LG TV with WiFi.Want me to help you build a cleaner "family video portal" page on your site that's more TV-friendly? Like bigger thumbnails, auto-play, and simple remote navigation?                                               Surfaces, blame it all on me. 

What about if I host it on on Vercel or the back end of one of my sites? Like, Render?

If you host the videos directly on Vercel or Render, your family can watch them on the LG TV through the browser — but there are real constraints you need to know:Vercel — not built for video hosting:Vercel is a frontend/edge platform. It can serve static files, but large video files will hit limits fastBandwidth: Vercel's free tier has 100GB/month. A few long family videos and you're done. Paid tiers get expensive for video fastFile size: Functions have payload limits; static files over ~50MB can be problematicNo streaming optimization: No adaptive bitrate, no transcoding. The browser downloads the whole file or tries to stream via HTTP range requests, which Vercel supports but not gracefully for videoRender — slightly better, still not ideal:Render's free tier has 100GB bandwidth/month tooYou can run a small web server (Node, Python, etc.) to serve filesStill no built-in video streaming infrastructure — just raw file servingDisk space on free tier is limited (512MB–1GB depending on plan)What actually works for family video on a budget:Table  Copy   ApproachSetupCostTV Experience Proton Drive links on your siteList links, they clickFree (your Proton plan)Opens Proton player, then cast to TVCloudflare R2Upload videos, get direct URLs, embed with <video>~$0.015/GB/month storage + egress feesNative browser playback, castableBackblaze B2Same as R2, slightly cheaper~$0.005/GB/month storageSameSelf-host on a cheap VPS (Hetzner, etc.)Nginx + your videos~$5/month for 20GB+Full control, direct URLsThe honest answer:
If you want your family to watch on an LG TV without friction, the simplest path is:Keep videos in Proton DrivePut shareable links on your Vercel site (just a clean list/page)They open the link on their phone → cast to LG TV via AirPlay/ChromecastIf you want true embedded playback inside your site on the TV, you need direct video URLs — which means moving off Proton Drive to R2, B2, or a VPS.What's your priority — zero cost, or a polished "Netflix-like" experience on the TV? Fly.io — better for this than Vercel/Render, but still not a video CDN.Fly.io runs containers close to users (edge deployment), so latency is low. But it's still general-purpose compute, not optimized for video streaming.The real issue on Fly.io:Bandwidth costs: ~$0.12/GB egress. Family videos are large. A 2GB video watched a few times = real money fastNo built-in storage: You'd need to attach a volume (persistent disk) or pull from external storageNo transcoding: If someone uploads a 4K .mov file, the LG TV browser may not play it. You'd need to handle format conversion yourselfWhat Fly.io is good for:Running a lightweight API or web server that serves video URLsProxying to cheap object storage (R2, B2) so you get edge-cached playback without paying Fly's bandwidth ratesBuilding a custom "family Netflix" app with auth, thumbnails, etc.Practical setup if you want to use Fly.io:plain   Copy [Your Fly.io app] → serves the web UI
         ↓
[Cloudflare R2 or B2] → stores actual video files, serves direct URLs
         ↓
[LG TV browser] → loads your Fly.io site, plays videos via <video src="R2-direct-url"> This way Fly.io only serves HTML/JS (tiny bandwidth), and R2/B2 handles the heavy video streaming at ~1/10th the cost.Bottom line: Fly.io is fine for the app, but don't store/serve raw video files from it unless you want a surprise bill. Pair it with cheap object storage for the videos.Want me to sketch out the actual architecture — Fly app + R2 + a simple TV-friendly frontend?
